Training against two objectives at once is the normal case, not the exception:
fit the new data **and** don't regress on the old, follow preferences **and**
stay capable, adapt to the target domain **and** keep the source. The default
move is to add the two losses and hand the sum to Adam [@kingma2015adam]. That
throws away the two things that actually matter — whether the tasks agreed on
this particular coordinate, and whether the batch was large enough to tell.

> Adam's per-coordinate step is an uncalibrated answer to the question *given
> what I measured, what is the probability that my true gradient agrees with
> me?* The calibrated answer is $\Phi$, the Gaussian CDF. Ask the same question
> about two tasks instead of one and you get **Adam2D**: an update that is
> guaranteed, in expectation, to descend on both.

The construction and the guarantees below come from [@dine2025improving], where
they were derived for one particular pair of tasks. Nothing in them depends on
that choice, so this post states them for two arbitrary tasks and drops the
application. The one-dimensional case is not a separate story either: it is the
same formula with one gradient measured exactly, so Adam falls out as a
degenerate case rather than sitting beside it as an analogy.

## What Adam actually computes

Write Adam per coordinate, dropping the bias correction:

$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\,\frac{\hat m_t}{\sqrt{\hat v_t} + \epsilon},
\qquad
\hat m_t = \mathrm{EMA}(\hat g_t), \quad \hat v_t = \mathrm{EMA}(\hat g_t^2).
$$ {#eq-adam}

Model the successive gradients of coordinate $i$ as $\hat g_t \sim
\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, i.i.d. — $\mu$ the true gradient, $\sigma$ the
measurement noise. Then $\E[\hat m_t] = \mu$ and $\E[\hat v_t] = \mu^2 +
\sigma^2$, so the multiplier in @eq-adam concentrates on

$$
\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{\mu^2 + \sigma^2}} \;=\; \frac{s}{\sqrt{1+s^2}}
\;=:\; \psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}(s),
\qquad s \doteq \frac{\mu}{\sigma}.
$$ {#eq-psi-adam}

Adam's step on a coordinate is **a function of that coordinate's
signal-to-noise ratio and nothing else**. This is the variance-adaptation
reading of [@balles2018dissecting]: $\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ is odd, maps $\R \to
(-1,1)$, is linear near the origin and tends to $\pm 1$, so Adam interpolates
between plain SGD at low SNR and signSGD [@bernstein2018signsgd] at high SNR.
The $\epsilon$ exists only to keep the ratio finite; it is not part of the idea.

A numerical check that @eq-psi-adam is not an artefact of the approximation —
simulating @eq-adam with $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$:

| $s$ | $\E[\hat m/\sqrt{\hat v}]$ (simulated) | $s/\sqrt{1+s^2}$ | $2\Phi(s)-1$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 0.102 | 0.100 | 0.080 |
| 0.5 | 0.456 | 0.447 | 0.383 |
| 1.0 | 0.704 | 0.707 | 0.683 |
| 2.0 | 0.894 | 0.894 | 0.955 |
| 5.0 | 0.980 | 0.981 | 1.000 |

## The question Adam answers without saying so

That multiplier is the answer to a question the algorithm never states. Stated,
the question is elementary:

> I measured $\hat g_i$ on this batch. What is the probability that the true
> gradient $\mu_i$ actually points the same way?

With a flat prior on the unknown $\mu_i$, the posterior is $\mu_i \mid \hat g_i
\sim \mathcal{N}(\hat g_i, \sigma_i^2)$ and the answer is immediate:

$$
p_i \;\doteq\; \mathbb{P}\!\left[\mu_i \hat g_i > 0 \,\middle|\, \hat g_i\right]
\;=\; \Phi\big(|s_i|\big) \;\in\; \left[\tfrac{1}{2},\, 1\right],
$$ {#eq-p1d}

with $\Phi$ the standard Gaussian CDF. **$p_i$ is the probability that I am
aligned with my own measurement**: $1/2$ when the batch told me nothing, $1$ when
the sign is beyond doubt. It is not a heuristic, it is the posterior. The signed
version is what a step should be proportional to,

$$
\psi(s) \;\doteq\; 2\Phi(s) - 1
\;=\; \operatorname{sign}(\hat g)\,\big(2p - 1\big)
\;=\; \E\!\left[\operatorname{sign}(\mu) \mid \hat g\right],
$$ {#eq-psi}

where $2p - 1 = \mathbb{P}[\text{aligned}] - \mathbb{P}[\text{anti-aligned}]$ is
the net evidence for the direction about to be taken. Nothing in @eq-psi is
tuned.

Now compare. Since $\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ also lands in $(-1,1)$, it too reads as
a probability, $\hat p_{\mathrm{Adam}} \doteq \tfrac{1}{2}(1 +
\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}(|s|))$ — Adam is *already* reporting a confidence that its
step direction is right. It is simply the wrong one:

| $s$ | $p = \Phi(s)$ (posterior) | $\hat p_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ | error |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.25 | 0.599 | 0.621 | $+0.023$ |
| 0.50 | 0.691 | 0.724 | $+0.032$ |
| 1.00 | 0.841 | 0.854 | $+0.012$ |
| 1.50 | 0.933 | 0.916 | $-0.017$ |
| 2.00 | 0.977 | 0.947 | $-0.030$ |
| 3.00 | 0.999 | 0.974 | $-0.024$ |
| 4.00 | 1.000 | 0.985 | $-0.015$ |

Adam is **overconfident below $s \approx 1.19$ and underconfident above it**. The
second failure is the severe one: its implicit confidence creeps toward $1$
polynomially and never arrives, so a coordinate whose sign is certain to seven
decimals is still treated as a $98.5\%$ bet.

::: {.light-content}
![](squashing-light.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](squashing-dark.svg)
:::

*Left: the two squashings against the per-coordinate SNR. Right: how fast each
commits to the sign. Adam's residual doubt decays polynomially, $1 -
\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}(s) \sim 1/2s^2$; the calibrated one decays like
$e^{-s^2/2}$.*

$\psi$ has every structural property of $\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ — odd, bounded by
$1$, linear at the origin ($\psi'(0) = \sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 0.80$ against $1$, a
constant the learning rate absorbs), sign in the limit — and one that
$\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ lacks: it is calibrated. The square root is a guess at the
shape of a function whose exact form the noise model already fixes.

## Two tasks

Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be two losses we want to decrease *simultaneously*, with no
hierarchy between them. Each is measured on its own batch, so each gradient is a
noisy estimate of the truth:

$$
\hat g_1 = g_1 + N_1, \quad N_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0; \Sigma_1),
\qquad
\hat g_2 = g_2 + N_2, \quad N_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0; \Sigma_2),
$$ {#eq-model}

with $N_1 \perp N_2$, $g_k \doteq \nabla L_k$, and per-coordinate SNRs
$s_{k,i} \doteq \hat g_{k,i} / \sigma_{k,i}$ where $\sigma_{k,i}^2 \doteq
\Sigma_{k,(i,i)}$. What we want from an update is exactly this:

::: {#def-aligned name="alignment with both tasks"}

&nbsp;

An update direction $\Delta$ is **aligned** with $L_1$ and $L_2$ at $\theta$ if

$$
\langle \Delta,\, g_1(\theta)\rangle \le 0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\langle \Delta,\, g_2(\theta)\rangle \le 0 ,
$$ {#eq-aligned}

i.e. it is a descent direction for both to first order.

:::

Summing the losses does not give this. $-(g_1 + g_2)$ is aligned with the sum by
construction and with neither task individually: any coordinate where the two
disagree is decided by whichever gradient happens to be larger, and the loser
moves the wrong way. The information needed to avoid that is *the sign of each
true gradient* — which is precisely the quantity @eq-psi estimates.

::: {#prp-focus name="the focus vector, and the identity"}

&nbsp;

Write $\varphi_k \doteq \Phi(\hat g_k / \sigma_k)$ component-wise. Then the
probability that the two *true* gradients agree in sign on coordinate $i$ is

$$
f_i \;\doteq\; \mathbb{P}\!\left[g_{1,i}\,g_{2,i} > 0 \,\middle|\, \hat g_1, \hat g_2\right]
\;=\; \varphi_{1,i}\varphi_{2,i} + (1-\varphi_{1,i})(1-\varphi_{2,i})
$$ {#eq-focus}

and, equivalently,

$$
\boxed{\;f_i \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\Big(1 + \psi(s_{1,i})\,\psi(s_{2,i})\Big).\;}
$$ {#eq-identity}

:::

@eq-focus is the probability itself; @eq-identity is one line from it —
substitute $\varphi = (1+\psi)/2$, the linear terms cancel, and only
$\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \psi\psi)$ survives. That line is the whole point. The gate is
**the product of two calibrated Adam multipliers**, rescaled from $[-1,1]$ to
$[0,1]$; equivalently $2f-1 = \E[\operatorname{sign}(g_1)\operatorname{sign}(g_2)
\mid \hat g_1, \hat g_2]$ is a per-coordinate *sign correlation* between the two
tasks. Adam asks "which way, and how sure am I?" once; Adam2D asks it twice and
multiplies the answers.

::: {.light-content}
![](gate-light.png)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](gate-dark.png)
:::

*The gate $f$ over the two SNRs. Along either axis one task carries no signal and
$f = \tfrac{1}{2}$: the coordinate is neither trusted nor blocked, just
half-stepped.*

### Adam is the degenerate case

The one-dimensional rule is not an analogy. Take @eq-focus and let the second
"task" be *the measurement itself* — a direction known without noise, so
$\sigma_2 \to 0$ and $\varphi_2 = \mathbb{1}[\hat g_1 > 0]$. Both branches
collapse onto the same value:

$$
f_i \;=\; \varphi_{1,i}\,\mathbb{1}[\hat g_{1,i} > 0] + (1 - \varphi_{1,i})\,\mathbb{1}[\hat g_{1,i} < 0]
\;=\; \Phi\big(|s_{1,i}|\big) \;=\; p_i ,
$$ {#eq-collapse}

which is exactly @eq-p1d. **Adam2D with one gradient measured exactly is
calibrated Adam.** The number of tasks is a parameter of the same formula, and
$n = 1$ is already in the family.

## The optimiser

Gate the aggregate gradient and step:

$$
\Delta \;\doteq\; -\,f \odot \big(\alpha \hat g_1 + \beta \hat g_2\big),
\qquad (\alpha, \beta) \in \R_+^2 ,
$$ {#eq-update}

```text
Adam2D — one step

Require: batch gradients  ĝ1, ĝ2 ∈ R^d
         noise scales     σ1, σ2 ∈ R^d₊     (see § Estimating σ)
         weights α, β > 0 ; learning rate η ; stability ε

  s1 ← ĝ1 / (σ1 + ε)                 # per-coordinate SNR, task 1
  s2 ← ĝ2 / (σ2 + ε)                 # per-coordinate SNR, task 2

  ψ1 ← 2Φ(s1) − 1                    # soft sign = E[sign(g1) | ĝ1]
  ψ2 ← 2Φ(s2) − 1

  f  ← (1 + ψ1 ⊙ ψ2) / 2             # focus: P[the two tasks agree]

  Δ  ← − f ⊙ (α·ĝ1 + β·ĝ2)           # gated aggregate
  θ  ← θ + η·Δ
```

Two backward passes per step, one per task — the same cost as any method that
looks at two gradients, and no more. The gate itself is $\mathcal{O}(d)$ and
recycles gradients already computed; in particular it needs no third gradient,
unlike saliency-based masking [@fan2024salun]. $\Phi$ is `erf` up to a rescaling,
so it is one vectorised call.

If you want the version where *every* quantity is a squashed SNR — the pure
Adam2D, where magnitudes as well as the gate come from the posterior — feed the
aggregate through the same soft sign:

$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\,
\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\big(1 + \psi(s_1)\psi(s_2)\big)}_{\text{gate}}
\odot
\underbrace{\big(\alpha\,\psi(s_1) + \beta\,\psi(s_2)\big)}_{\text{direction}} .
$$ {#eq-2dadam}

### What the gate does at the corners

| regime | $f$ | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| both variances $\to 0$ | $\{0,1\}$ | the hard AND-mask [@parascandolo2020learning] on the measured gradients |
| both variances $\to \infty$ | $1/2$ | halve the learning rate, change nothing else |
| one task uninformative | $1/2$ | abstain, half-step |
| second gradient noiseless | $\Phi(|s|)$ | calibrated Adam, @eq-collapse |
| $L_2 = L_1$ on a second batch | $\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\psi(s)^2)$ | one task, gated by whether two batches agree |

Two structural properties are worth stating on their own. First, $f \ge 0$
always, so the gate can attenuate a coordinate but never flip it: unlike
projection-based conflict resolution [@yu2020gradient; @liu2021conflict], the
update is a non-negative reweighting of the aggregate and never rotates it into
a direction the aggregate did not propose. Second, $f \in [0,1]$ by
construction, so the pathology Adam's $\epsilon$ patches — a vanishing
denominator blowing up a step — has no analogue here.

The last two rows are the one-dimensional collapses, and they differ in what
plays the second opinion. Trusting the measurement gives calibrated Adam;
asking a second batch gives a strictly more conservative gate, since two noisy
votes agree less often than one noisy vote agrees with itself (at $s=1$: $0.733$
against $0.841$). Either way the effective learning rate ranges over $[\eta/2,
\eta]$ with the confidence of the coordinate — a milder, better-motivated
variant of the $\epsilon$ hack.

## The guarantee

Gating is only interesting if it still descends. It does, on **both** tasks.

::: {#prp-guarantee name="alignment in expectation"}

&nbsp;

Let $\alpha, \beta > 0$ and suppose the measured gradients are scalarly
independent in expectation, $\E[\langle \hat g_1, \hat g_2\rangle] = 0$. Then
$\Delta$ of @eq-update is aligned with both tasks in the sense of @def-aligned,
in expectation, and for any sufficiently small $\eta > 0$:

$$
\E\big[L_1(\theta + \eta \Delta)\big] \le L_1(\theta),
\qquad
\E\big[L_2(\theta + \eta \Delta)\big] \le L_2(\theta).
$$ {#eq-guarantee}

:::

This is the selling point, and the mechanism is visible in one expansion.
Alignment with $L_1$ needs $\langle \Delta, \hat g_1\rangle \le 0$, i.e.

$$
\alpha \sum_i f_i\, \hat g_{1,i}^2 \;+\; \beta \sum_i f_i\, \hat g_{1,i}\hat g_{2,i}
\;\ge\; 0 .
$$ {#eq-expansion}

The first sum is non-negative for free, because $f \ge 0$ — that is the entire
value of a gate that cannot change signs. Only the cross term needs an argument,
and the cheapest one available suffices: two random vectors in high dimension
have vanishing inner product [@dine2025improving]. The statement is symmetric in
$1 \leftrightarrow 2$, so both tasks are covered by the same line.

The hypothesis is in fact stronger than necessary, in a direction worth noting.
The cross term in @eq-expansion is not the plain inner product but the
$f$-weighted one, and $f$ is by construction *large exactly where the product
$\hat g_{1,i}\hat g_{2,i}$ is positive*. The weighting is positively associated
with what it weights, so the sum should be biased upward rather than merely
vanish. A simulation — $d = 4000$ coordinates, true gradients drawn
independently, heterogeneous noise scales, $600$ draws — is unambiguous:

```python
phi_1, phi_2 = norm.cdf(gh_1 / s_1), norm.cdf(gh_2 / s_2)
f = phi_1 * phi_2 + (1 - phi_1) * (1 - phi_2)
cross_weighted = np.sum(f * gh_1 * gh_2)   # > 0 in 600 / 600 draws
cross_plain    = np.dot(gh_1, gh_2)        # straddles 0, mean ~ 0
```

The unweighted inner product straddles zero as advertised; the $f$-weighted one
was positive in every draw, and both $\langle g_1, \Delta\rangle$ and $\langle
g_2, \Delta\rangle$ were negative in every draw. So @prp-guarantee holds with
room to spare, and the honest statement is that the gate *helps* the guarantee
rather than needing an assumption to survive it. Turning "positively associated"
into a proof — an FKG-type inequality on the concordance of $f$ with $\hat g_1
\odot \hat g_2$ — is open.

There is also a trust region. For all $q \ge 1$,

$$
\|\theta' - \theta\|_q \;\le\; \eta\,\|f\|_0^{1/q}\,\|\Delta\|_\infty ,
$$ {#eq-vicinity}

so each step is controlled by how many coordinates the gate actually opens — and
in practice that number falls as training proceeds.

## Where this applies

Any setting with two losses and no principled way to weigh them:

- **Multi-task learning** — two task losses, the canonical gradient-conflict
  setting [@yu2020gradient; @liu2021conflict].
- **Fine-tuning without regression** — new-data loss against a retention loss on
  the original distribution.
- **Alignment against capability** — a preference or safety objective against
  the base language-modelling loss.
- **Continual learning** — current task against a replay buffer.
- **Domain adaptation** — source and target losses.
- **Constrained training** — a main loss against a fairness or sparsity penalty.
- **Unlearning** — a forgetting objective against a retention objective, the
  case the construction was originally derived for [@dine2025improving].

The gate never has to be told which task matters more. That decision stays in
$(\alpha, \beta)$, where it belongs; $f$ only reports how much the two tasks
actually agree, coordinate by coordinate.

## Estimating $\sigma$

Everything above needs the per-coordinate noise scale $\sigma_{k,i}$, and this is
where an implementation can quietly lose the plot. The convenient shortcut is to
read Adam's second moment $\hat v$, which is free if you are running Adam anyway.
But $\hat v$ estimates $\mu^2 + \sigma^2$, not $\sigma^2$, and it describes the
noise of a *single datum*, not of the batch mean. Two consequences:

1. **A squashed quantity fed into a squashing function.** The argument handed to
   $\Phi$ is then close to $\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}(s)$, an $O(1)$ number, so
   $\varphi$ rarely leaves $(\Phi(-1), \Phi(1)) = (0.16, 0.84)$ and $f$ rarely
   leaves $(0.27, 0.73)$. The gate works, but at low contrast. Divide by an
   estimate of $\sigma$ alone — the AdaBelief statistic $\hat v - \hat m^2$
   [@zhuang2020adabelief] — and the SNR is unbounded again, so the gate can
   saturate.
2. **Blindness to batch size.** The noise on a mean of $B$ samples is
   $\sigma/\sqrt{B}$, so the correct argument is $\sqrt{B}\,\hat g/\hat\sigma$.
   Otherwise doubling the batch buys no extra confidence — which is exactly the
   quantity the method claims to reason about.

Both point at the same replacement,

$$
\varphi_k \;\leftarrow\; \Phi\!\left(\lambda\,\sqrt{B}\;\frac{\hat g_k}{\sqrt{\hat v_k - \hat m_k^2}}\right),
$$ {#eq-fix}

with $\lambda$ a temperature. At $B = 256$ the factor $\sqrt{B} = 16$ will
saturate the gate into the hard AND-mask, so $\lambda$ is doing real work — but
it is one interpretable hyperparameter on a scale where $\lambda = 1$ is the
statistically honest setting and anything else is a deliberate hedge against the
Gaussian model being wrong.

## Open questions

- **Q1. More than two tasks.** The closed form generalises immediately:
  $\mathbb{P}[\text{all } n \text{ agree}] = \prod_k \varphi_k + \prod_k (1 -
  \varphi_k)$, which decays to $2^{1-n}$ and gates everything shut for moderate
  $n$. Pairwise gates, or a soft-OR over pairs, are the obvious repairs; which
  one keeps @prp-guarantee is not obvious.
- **Q2. Proving the association.** Does $\mathrm{Cov}(f_i, \hat g_{1,i}\hat
  g_{2,i}) \ge 0$ hold in general under @eq-model? Simulation says yes,
  emphatically; a proof would let @prp-guarantee drop its hypothesis entirely.
- **Q3. Does calibration pay off in plain 1D training?** The tail argument says
  a calibrated Adam should behave like signSGD sooner, and the calibration table
  says it should be markedly less timid above $s \approx 1.2$. That is a cheap
  experiment on a standard benchmark and I have not run it.
- **Q4. Beyond Gaussian.** @eq-model is the one modelling choice in the whole
  construction, and gradient noise is famously heavier-tailed. Swapping $\Phi$
  for a Student-$t$ CDF changes nothing structurally — @eq-identity survives any
  symmetric noise family — but it changes the tail, which is where all the
  action is.
